notes: Replaced cli-update-one-major-step with cli-update-code-migrations to avoid a false statement based on a changed number. Refined cli-workspace-shared-configuration to test how project build settings apply within a workspace.

cards.statement: After adding @angular/ssr, Angular CLI prerenders application routes by default during a production build.
cards.explanation: Adding @angular/ssr initially configures prerendered pages. Request-time rendering is selected through the server route configuration.

cards.statement: Angular executes a route's getPrerenderParams function during the build to choose its prerendered parameter values.
cards.explanation: getPrerenderParams supplies parameter combinations for generating static route documents during the build.

cards.statement: During server rendering, Angular exposes the browser's window global to component constructors.
cards.explanation: The browser's window global is unavailable to component code executing during server rendering.
cards.misconception: Angular supplies browser globals while executing component code on the server.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular creates a fresh value for a top-level useValue provider for each request.
cards.explanation: Top-level useValue values persist across server requests. Angular establishes those values when the application code is first evaluated.
cards.misconception: Angular initializes top-level useValue values separately for incoming server requests.

cards.statement: During prerendering, Angular supplies REQUEST with a Request representing the page being generated.
cards.explanation: REQUEST has the value null during prerendering because that build-time render has no incoming HTTP request.
cards.misconception: Prerendering creates an incoming request object for injection through REQUEST.

cards.statement: With SSR and hydration enabled, Angular reuses DOM nodes produced by the server render.
cards.explanation: Hydration connects the application to the existing server-rendered DOM instead of rebuilding that DOM from scratch.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular automatically hydrates a component even when its server and client DOM structures differ.
cards.explanation: Hydration expects matching server and client DOM structure, including Angular's generated comments and whitespace.
cards.misconception: Hydration reconciles differing server and client component structures.

cards.statement: In Angular v22.1 with SSR, the transfer cache stores GET requests with withCredentials: true by default.
cards.explanation: Angular's default HTTP transfer cache excludes credential-bearing requests. Setting withCredentials: true makes a request ineligible under that default.
cards.misconception: The default transfer cache includes credential-bearing GET requests.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer-cache eligibility defaults changed in v22.1 and may change in later releases.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, provideClientHydration enables incremental hydration by default with SSR.
cards.explanation: Incremental hydration is part of the hydration provider's default feature set rather than a separate opt-in.
cards.volatilityNote: This hydration default changed in v22 and could be revised in a later major release.

cards.statement: On later client navigation with SSR, Angular loads new @defer views using hydrate triggers.
cards.explanation: Hydrate triggers govern the initial server-rendered load. A new view rendered by later client navigation uses its regular defer triggers.
cards.misconception: Hydrate triggers govern new deferred views during subsequent client navigation.

cards.statement: With SSR, Angular keeps nested @defer blocks dehydrated beneath a parent marked `hydrate never` on initial load.
cards.explanation: On the initial server-rendered load, a parent marked hydrate never blocks hydration throughout its nested subtree.

cards.statement: In Angular v22 with SSR, Angular responds to unrecognized Host headers with 400 Bad Request.
cards.explanation: Angular's server pipeline rejects unrecognized hostnames. The allowedHosts option configures which hostnames it accepts.
cards.volatilityNote: Angular's built-in host validation behavior and configuration may evolve in later releases.

cards.statement: Angular CLI propagates a project's build options to sibling projects in the same workspace.
cards.explanation: angular.json holds separate project configurations with their own build targets and options. Editing one project's options does not change its siblings' options.
cards.misconception: A project's build options configure sibling projects through the shared workspace.

cards.statement: Angular's documentation recommends fixture.whenStable() over fixture.detectChanges() in zoneless tests.
cards.explanation: Waiting for stability lets Angular respond to real change notifications. detectChanges() forces a check that the application might not schedule.

cards.statement: ng update leaves source-code migrations to the developer after updating Angular package versions.
cards.explanation: ng update runs applicable migration schematics, which can transform application code as part of the dependency update.
cards.misconception: ng update changes dependency versions while developers perform its code migrations manually.

cards.statement: New Angular CLI applications use the application builder by default for their build system.
cards.explanation: The CLI configures new applications with the stable application builder; existing workspaces may need a migration to adopt it.

cards.statement: With SSR, the application builder requires a separate server builder to compile the application's server code.
cards.explanation: The application builder integrates server compilation with the application build, including configured prerendering.
cards.misconception: The application builder handles client code while a separate builder compiles its SSR server.

cards.statement: Angular CLI uses Vite to bundle application code for an optimized production build.
cards.explanation: Angular uses Vite to serve development builds produced by its build system. The application builder uses esbuild for bundling.
cards.misconception: Angular delegates production application bundling to Vite.

cards.statement: Since Angular v22, Angular marks the webpack builders in @angular-devkit/build-angular as deprecated.
cards.explanation: Angular v22 marks @angular-devkit/build-angular's webpack builders as deprecated and directs projects toward @angular/build.
cards.volatilityNote: Deprecated webpack builders may be removed in a future Angular major release.

cards.statement: In Angular v21 and later, Angular CLI uses Vitest by default for unit tests in new projects.
cards.explanation: Angular CLI configures a new project's test setup for Vitest when the developer accepts the default runner choice.

cards.statement: Angular's default Vitest setup runs component tests directly in a real browser process.
cards.explanation: Angular's default Vitest setup runs unit tests in Node.js and uses jsdom to simulate browser DOM APIs.
cards.misconception: The default Angular Vitest configuration launches a browser for component tests.

cards.statement: In Angular v22, TestBed uses zoneless change detection by default even when zone.js is loaded.
cards.explanation: Loading zone.js does not choose TestBed's change-detection mode. Its default test environment remains zoneless.

cards.statement: TestBed.createComponent() evaluates template bindings synchronously before returning its fixture.
cards.explanation: TestBed.createComponent() constructs a fixture and component but does not run change detection synchronously to evaluate template bindings.
cards.misconception: Fixture creation completes an initial synchronous template check.

cards.statement: With DeferBlockBehavior.Manual, tests render a @defer block's loading state through its DeferBlockFixture.
cards.explanation: Configure Manual behavior in TestBed, obtain the block fixture, and call render(DeferBlockState.Loading) to select the loading state.
